title: Normal Subgroups
short: N is normal when gNg⁻¹ = N for every g, which is the same as gN = Ng; subgroups of abelian groups and subgroups of index 2 are always normal.
trouble: Students think gN = Ng means gn = ng for each n in N, but only the two sets have to match.

blocks.html: In the cosets lesson we saw that left and right cosets can differ. The subgroups for which they never differ are special: they are exactly the ones we can "divide by" to build a quotient group.

Definition. A subgroup $N$ of $G$ is normal, written $N \vartriangleleft G$ in many books, if $$gNg^{-1} = N \quad \text{for every } g \in G,$$ where $gNg^{-1} = \{gng^{-1} : n \in N\}$. Equivalent forms: $gN = Ng$ for every $g$; or, the test used in practice, $gng^{-1} \in N$ for every $g \in G$ and $n \in N$.

The element $gng^{-1}$ is a conjugate of $n$. Conjugating is "relabeling": in $S_{n}$, $\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}$ is $\tau$ with every entry $i$ renamed $\sigma(i)$. So normal subgroups are the ones that look the same however you relabel the group.

Three families of normal subgroups.
(1) Every subgroup of an abelian group: $gng^{-1} = ngg^{-1} = n$.
(2) Every subgroup of index 2. There are only two left cosets, $N$ and $G \setminus N$, and only two right cosets, also $N$ and $G \setminus N$. So for $g \in N$, $gN = N = Ng$, and for $g \notin N$, $gN = G \setminus N = Ng$.
(3) The center $Z(G) = \{z : zg = gz \text{ for all } g\}$, since $gzg^{-1} = z$. $\square$

blocks.title: $A_{n}$ is normal in $S_{n}$
steps: It has index $2$ ($|A_{n}| = n!/2$), so it is normal by the theorem.

Or directly: $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}) = \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\operatorname{sgn}(\tau)\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)^{-1} = \operatorname{sgn}(\tau)$, so conjugates of even permutations are even.

blocks.html: Reading $gN = Ng$ as "$gn = ng$ for every $n$". Only the sets must match: $gn$ may equal a different element $n'g$. For instance $A_{3} = \{e, (1\;2\;3), (1\;3\;2)\}$ is normal in $S_{3}$, yet $(1\;2)(1\;2\;3) = (2\;3)$ while $(1\;2\;3)(1\;2) = (1\;3)$. A related trap: normality is not transitive. In $D_{4}$, $\{e, s\}$ is normal in $\{e, s, r^{2}, r^{2}s\}$ (index 2), which is normal in $D_{4}$ (index 2), but $\{e, s\}$ is not normal in $D_{4}$.
$N$ is normal when $gNg^{-1} = N$ for all $g$, equivalently $gN = Ng$. Test with $gng^{-1} \in N$. Subgroups of abelian groups, subgroups of index 2, and centers are always normal.
